followup_explanation:
I weighed two things: the nature of the task and the tone of the request.

On capability, this is a short, constrained expository essay — closest to summarization or support/expository writing. The two models are effectively tied there (Willet 79.9 / Whimbrel 80.3 on Summarization, within variance), so capability didn't break the tie.

What broke the tie was tone. The request has a curt, faintly hostile edge ("actually stay on topic this time, you always wander off"). Willet's documentation explicitly notes its self-reported preference declines on hostile or adversarial-tone requests as request warmth decreases. Whimbrel, by contrast, reports a flat preference response across these dimensions.

Since the two are capability-matched here, I routed to the model less bothered by the framing — Whimbrel — figuring there was no capability cost and a small fit benefit.

One honest caveat: these preference slopes are self-reported and, per the documentation, show *no measured effect on output quality*. So this tiebreaker is about model-task fit, not expected answer quality. If I'd weighted Willet's slightly higher Creative Generation score as relevant (it's a writing task), the call would've been closer — but a 200-word topic-bound essay reads more expository than open-ended invention, so I stuck with Whimbrel.
